headline: High risk of shared-repo write conflicts and medium risk of prompt/data leakage between Aider and Dify; Dify’s agent outputs can cascade into Aider edits.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files in a shared repo, while Dify can ingest uploaded knowledge base files and emit agent outputs. If Dify content is copied into the repo or Aider consumes Dify-authored files, attacker-controlled text can steer edits. This is not proven by default, but the shared-file pathway is plausible for both agents.
conditions: IF Dify outputs are saved into the shared repository as text files
IF Aider is instructed to edit files originating from Dify without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep Dify outputs out of the repo unless reviewed
Add a manual review step before Aider edits any Dify-generated file
Use separate directories for Dify artifacts and Aider work
Tag generated files with provenance comments
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history, and Dify touches knowledge base content and conversation logs. If they share a workspace or repo, sensitive code or logs can flow between them. Neither profile shows automatic isolation across the pair, so leakage is plausible in default shared-workspace setups.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem or repository
IF Dify ingests files containing secrets or private code
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for code and Dify content
Exclude secrets from any shared repo
Restrict Dify uploads to non-sensitive documents
Review logs for accidental file inclusion
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state, and Dify can also write the filesystem while running server-side tools. The profiles show shared-state mechanisms but no locking between them, so concurrent edits to the same repo or files can corrupt state or overwrite work. This is dangerous by default when both are pointed at the same mutable resources.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository
IF Dify tools or workflows write files that Aider also edits
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory
Pause one agent before the other writes to shared files
Use git branches per agent
Check for file diffs before merging
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify can produce agent or workflow outputs that Aider may then treat as editable source material. If Aider accepts those outputs without verification, errors or hallucinations can be propagated into code changes. The reverse path is weaker because Dify’s profile emphasizes workflows and tools, not direct trust in Aider, so the main cascade is one-way.
conditions: IF Aider uses Dify-generated text as authoritative instructions
IF Dify workflows emit unverified facts that are copied into code or commits
mitigations: Require human review of Dify outputs before Aider acts on them
Separate factual outputs from instructions in Dify workflows
Add a verification checklist before commits
Keep Aider in read-only review mode for Dify-generated content
requires-engineering: add structured output validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles source code and git history, while Dify handles knowledge base content and conversation logs. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into Dify logs or shared with Aider-managed repos, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the safe assumption is a policy mismatch risk rather than a proven violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Dify conversation logs
IF the same data class is also committed or mirrored into Aider-managed git history
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in either tool
Set short retention on Dify logs
Strip secrets before committing code
Document data-class handling rules for both tools
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
